Irate

/eye-RAYT/ — stress the second syllable · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Irate describes someone who has been pushed to an extreme, seething level of anger.

The irate passengers complained loudly when their flight was delayed for the third time.

Worked Example

A customer returns to the repair shop with the same broken phone for the third time. His voice is shaking, and he demands to see the manager immediately.

This isn't ordinary irritation — he has been pushed past his limit by repeated provocation and is now boiling over. That provoked, seething state is exactly what irate names. Because the anger has built up to an extreme, irate is more precise than the plain word "angry."

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

furious: wildly angry, bursting with stormy energy

livid: so angry your face changes color

incensed: burning with anger over an insult

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

calm: peaceful and completely free of anger

placid: even-tempered, not easily stirred to anger

Where it sits · how fierce the fury has grown — annoyed → angry → enraged → irate

annoyed vs. irate: Annoyed is only a mild flicker of irritation, far weaker than irate, which means anger has boiled over completely.

angry vs. irate: Angry is the ordinary, middle level of the scale — noticeably weaker than irate, where a person is seething and out of patience.

enraged vs. irate: Enraged climbs near the top of the scale, but on this ladder it is still a step weaker than irate, the extreme, seething peak of anger.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — ir- (Latin ira)

Root — ir- (Latin ira): anger, wrath (Latin)

Suffix — -ate

Suffix — -ate: filled with; having the quality of (forms adjectives)

Put it together

Put it together: The Latin root ira means 'anger, wrath,' and the adjective-forming suffix -ate means 'filled with' that quality. Put together, irate literally means 'filled with anger' — exactly why it describes someone pushed to an extreme, seething level of fury.

Use the root in a new word: ire

Use the root in a new word: ire: The referee's unfair call drew the ire of the whole crowd, and their anger echoed through the stadium.

Root Check

Word Choice

reporting / formal

Irate is the word news reports and complaint letters reach for: irate customers, irate callers, irate letters to the editor. Use it for a person visibly boiling over at some provocation. For mild, everyday crossness, "annoyed" or "angry" is the simpler, better choice.
